summary_statistics.highest_priority_action: Four things, in this order, and the first one is free. (1) BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, SEND THE STAFF MESSAGE - today, in one paragraph: nobody from Microsoft, your IT provider or your service desk will ring to ask for a password, an MFA code or a sign-in approval about Friday's outage, and here is the one internal number to verify any such call. Criminals were phoning UK taxpayers for their HMRC usernames and passwords within hours of the 13 November Microsoft 365 outage; HMRC posted its warning at 11:55 UTC, the NCSC warned about IT-helpdesk impersonation, and at least one council reported the same calls. Then hunt identity telemetry for 13-14 November: MFA or device registrations with no matching help-desk ticket, password resets following an inbound call, successful sign-ins from a first-seen country, and remote-support tools (Quick Assist, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, Zoho Assist) started during or after the outage. Require callback verification on every help-desk credential reset and retrospectively audit the ones performed on Friday. (2) ASK YOUR MSP TWO QUESTIONS, IN WRITING, TODAY: does any provider with remote access to your estate run N-able N-central, and is its Legacy API enabled? And does any of them run ConnectWise ScreenConnect, cloud-hosted, with an 'RMM+' family extension installed? For N-central, disabling the Legacy API is the control that removes exposure to the 4EverAble2Shell chain; Hotfix 2 is not a fix - 19 of 21 reported compromised servers were already on it - and if the Legacy API was ever internet-reachable, hunt from 11 November for an xvd.service systemd unit, files under /tmp/.xvd or /var/tmp/.xvd and miner processes, and treat a miner as a pre-ransomware foothold with downstream customer exposure rather than as a nuisance. For ScreenConnect, disable RMM+ extensions in on-premises deployments yourself, reconcile every installed client against your authorised instance identifier, hunt Defender exclusions added in the last fortnight, and do NOT triage a suspected infection by connecting through ScreenConnect - Microsoft's 13 November analysis describes the toolkit targeting technician sessions, so the responder's own workstation is in scope. Treat a non-answer from a provider as a yes. (3) KEV: TWO DEADLINES ARE NOW OVERDUE AND TWO MORE FALL ON 16 NOVEMBER. Overdue since 13 November: Barracuda ESG (CVE-2026-116606 + CVE-2026-111560, patch to 9.4.0.030 or later) and Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 (25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6) - if you patched Ivanti on 13 October you covered only CVE-2026-104935, the Integrity Checker Tool can return clean on a compromised appliance because attacker commands run in memory, and anything reachable from an appliance exposed since 3 October needs LAPS rotation and BitLocker re-escrow. The 9 November batch (GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, OpenSSH, IBM Aspera Faspex) has been overdue since 12 November. Due 16 November: Check Point CVE-2026-123039 - apply the November Jumbo Hotfix (R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132, R81.20 Take 174 or later) and note that CISA requires forensic triage under BOD 26-04, so patching alone is not compliance and any Mobile Access portal exposed and unpatched since mid-October needs a compromise assessment, with the campaign's destructive objective making offline or immutable virtualisation backups and a tested restore the thing that actually matters - and UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713 (upgrade to 6.2.7.1; on 5.x blacklist the labeled-response module and restart). Due 24 November: Cisco BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320 (RI.2026.07, and rotate the system identity key, certificates and stored credentials because key material read through an XXE stays valid after patching), Openwave, Chrome 157.0.8103.50+ (force a relaunch, not just a download) and Outlook CVE-2026-124194 (verify Office build numbers rather than OS patch level, and block outbound SMB/445 and WebDAV). (4) GITHUB AND CI SECRETS, PUBLIC SECTOR ESPECIALLY: search every organisation you control for pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes', rotate every Actions secret in any repository touched since 10 November, and constrain GitHub OIDC trust policies to specific repositories and branches - the wfx-loot stealer exchanges OIDC tokens for live AWS, Azure and GCP sessions, GitHub's hold on the malicious workflows was bypassed through an npm hook, and anything caught by October's GhostAction campaign is more likely to be in scope again. UK public-sector bodies should continue the secret-scanning work across the 349 public repositories in the ControlPlane survey and treat every secret ever committed as compromised rather than merely revoked: the Planning Inspectorate's Entra ID credential sat in a public repository for 18 months, and the agency's own finding of no breach rests on no monitoring of a credential nobody knew was exposed.
